description: We are a collective, not just a team.  We start with little, build fast and learn by doing. No bosses, no egos: just ideas, code and a shared goal. We believe in sharing, open source and technology that serves people. Our resources are limited, our curiosity is not. Want to build instead of watch? Join the movement.
summary:
Martian Map is a web tool that helps a two-person crew plan and carry out a safe, science-driven walk on Mars. Existing tools such as Mars Trek show the planet at regional or global scale; we zoom in on a 2 × 2 km area of the Mount Sharp boxwork formations that Curiosity explored in 2025, and layer NASA data at 1 m resolution: HiRISE imagery, a 1 m terrain model, slope and roughness hazards, a ridge-and-hollow map of the boxworks, Curiosity's real traverse, and radiation and weather measured on site by Curiosity.
A least-time route algorithm plans a 1.57 km loop from the pressurized rover to two contrasting science targets, a ridge and a hollow, while avoiding unsafe terrain. Our hazard model is calibrated against the tilt that Curiosity actually measured at 73 positions in the area (mean error reduced from 7.6° to 2.8°). The same tool runs inside the rover for planning and as a simplified walk mode for a helmet heads-up display, so the crew can navigate on their own despite the 3 to 22 minute communication delay with Earth.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Martian Map plans one specific surface excursion: “Sortie 01”, a Marswalk through the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons, Gale crater). Following NASA's preliminary Mars mission studies, we assume two astronauts on the surface, living in a pressurized rover parked on flat, safe ground, and always walking in pairs. The tool shows them where to go, what is dangerous, what is worth studying, how long it will take and how much radiation they will receive.

  • Planning mode (inside the rover): a 2D map and a 3D terrain view of the 2 × 2 km area with switchable layers (HiRISE imagery, shaded relief, slopes, hazards, ridges and hollows, Curiosity's traverse), the route split into stages with distance, climb, maximum slope and walking time, an elevation profile, and a conditions panel (radiation, temperature, pressure, wind, dust).
  • Walk mode (helmet heads-up display): a minimal screen with the heading to the next waypoint, distance and time to it, time left before returning to the rover, the slope under the astronaut's feet and a hazard alert.
  • Shared views: the same link opens a surface crew, orbiting crew or mission control view, so everyone works from the same map.

Science objective

Boxworks are networks of ridges up to several kilometres across, visible from orbit on Mount Sharp. Curiosity found that ridges and the hollows between them have different mineralogy, traces of the last groundwater on Mars. Our walk therefore visits two contrasting targets: a ridge (Target A) and a hollow (Target B).

How does it work?

  1. Area of interest: we extracted Curiosity's 73 real positions in the boxwork area (sols 4534 to 4830) from NASA/JPL's MMGIS service and centred a 2 × 2 km study area on them.
  2. Data extraction: with GDAL/rasterio we read only this area from the USGS 1 m terrain model and the HiRISE colour mosaic of Gale crater (multi-gigabyte files), and reproject everything to the same Mars coordinate frame so that all layers align exactly.
  3. Hazards: slope and terrain roughness are computed from the terrain model. Slopes are classified as easy (under 10°), caution (10 to 20°) and no-go (over 20° or very rough ground).
  4. Validation against reality: we compared our computed slopes with the tilt Curiosity actually measured at its 73 positions. Smoothing the terrain at a 5 m scale reduced the mean error from 7.6° to 2.8° (computed mean 8.7° vs. 8.5° measured). The no-go roughness threshold is set just above the roughest ground Curiosity crossed.
  5. Science targets: a topographic position index (elevation minus local average) maps ridges and hollows; the tool picks the clearest ridge and the clearest hollow near Curiosity's path, outside no-go zones.
  6. Route: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm runs on a 4 m grid where each cell costs the time needed to cross it, using Tobler's hiking function (walking speed as a function of slope). No-go cells are excluded. Result: a 1.57 km loop, 88 m of climb, 27 minutes at hiking speed and 54 minutes in a cautious spacesuit scenario, with only 13% of the path in caution terrain although 25% of the area is no-go.
  7. Radiation: using the surface dose measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument (0.67 mSv per day), the walk adds about 0.024 mSv.

What benefits does it have?

  • Hyperlocal: the scale of one walk, which global tools do not cover.
  • Grounded in real measurements: the hazard model is checked against a rover that actually drove the terrain.
  • Autonomy: the crew can navigate without waiting for Earth, as signals take 3 to 22 minutes each way.
  • Light and reusable: a web page that runs in any browser; the pipeline can generate a new mission for any area that has a terrain model.

What do we hope to achieve?

Next steps: add orbital mineralogy (CRISM) and thermal inertia (THEMIS) layers, live data from the crew rover's own weather station, offline use, and a version for Earth explorers in hostile terrain such as equatorial forests or deserts, using NASA Earth observation data.

Assumptions and limits: the cautious walking speed (half of hiking speed in a suit), the 10° and 20° slope thresholds and the radiation average (2012–2013) are adjustable parameters, not certified values.

Tools and languages: Python (GDAL/rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow) in Google Colab for the data pipeline; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the interface; hosted at martian-map.devs-solutions.tech.

Team DevSec, Libreville, Gabon: Gédéon Mouloundi Mayagha, Leila Kiena Pambo, Mbenda prince, Orval Lanydeh.
